## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Vikaṇṇajātaka* (Ja 233) is a canonical Jātaka tale belonging to the Pali *Khuddakanikāya* [SuttaCentral]. According to the narrative framework preserved in its tradition, the Buddha recounted the story while residing at Jetavana with reference to a backsliding monk [SuttaCentral].

The verse text features an admonition regarding one who has been fatally pierced in a vital spot (*mammamhi*) by a barbed arrow or barb (*vikaṇṇakena*), having been struck down on account of food and music while greedily pursuing fish (*lolo ca macche anubandhamāno*) [Fausböll 1879]. The prose commentary explains *vikaṇṇakena* as referring to a barbed dart or arrow (*vikaṇṇakasallena*) that delivers an incurable wound [Fausböll 1879].

In terms of parallels and text reuse, machine analysis by DharmaNexus records seven matching passages shared internally with the commentary in the second volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Dutiyo bhāgo), covering the canonical verses alongside their narrative and exegesis [DharmaNexus; Fausböll 1879]. DharmaNexus records no cross-language parallels in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan corpora [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral lists four translations across four languages [SuttaCentral].
